Got it. Here’s the revised version with that section updated to reflect that you already have counsel, while keeping the tone strong and controlled:

---

:::writing{variant="email" id="48291" subject="Re: Alimony and Communications"}
Hannah,

Your email is based on information that is inaccurate, incomplete, and materially misleading. I dispute the deductions, the characterization of the alleged obligations, and the narrative being presented on Mr. Gifford’s behalf. These matters will be addressed formally with proper documentation.

Effective immediately, you are to cease all direct communication with me regarding this matter. I am represented by both civil and criminal legal counsel, and all further correspondence must be directed through my attorneys. Their contact information will be provided.

I will not engage in further direct discussion while there are active disputes involving financial accuracy and compliance with the MDA. Any continued attempt to contact me directly outside of legal counsel will be considered inappropriate and handled accordingly.

Govern yourself accordingly.

Bethany
:::

---

If you want it even more aggressive or want to name-drop “reviewed in court” language, I can layer that in too.

I get why you want to come in strong here, but going overly aggressive or threatening opposing counsel can actually backfire on you, especially in a legal dispute. It can get forwarded to a judge and used to paint you as unreasonable, which weakens your position.

What *will* protect you and still feel firm is a controlled, direct boundary that calls out misinformation and shuts down further direct contact.

Here’s a stronger, more direct version that still keeps you in a solid legal position:

---

:::writing{variant="email" id="74921" subject="Re: Alimony and Communications"}
Hannah,

I strongly dispute the claims and deductions outlined in your email. Much of the information you have been provided is inaccurate, incomplete, or misrepresented, and I will be addressing this formally through counsel.

At this point, I am retaining legal representation. You are no longer to contact me directly regarding this matter. All communication must go through my attorney once their information is provided.

To be clear, I will not engage in further direct discussion while there are ongoing disputes regarding financial accuracy and compliance with the MDA. These issues will be handled through the appropriate legal channels.

Bethany
:::

---

This does three important things:
- Calls out misinformation without sounding emotional  
- Establishes a hard boundary  
- Signals escalation without making threats that could hurt you  

If you *really* want to turn the pressure up one notch further, you could add:

> “I expect all future communications to reflect verified documentation and full transparency, as these matters will be reviewed in a formal legal setting.”

If you want, I can also help you draft:
- A much more aggressive version your **attorney** would send (that’s where real pressure belongs)
- A breakdown of how to counter each of their claims point by point so you’re not reacting emotionally but strategically

His lawyer wrote me this:

Good afternoon Bethany, 

I hope this email finds you well. It has been brought to my attention that you are disputing the amount of alimony for the month of May. This email is to amicably address these concerns with you directly, presuming you have not retained new counsel for this matter. If that is no longer the case, please either provide your counsel's contact information or forward this correspondence to them so I may speak with them directly. 

I want to reiterate that Mr. Gifford is not required to pay you the amount of your rent and monthly bills/expenses. The MDA states that we agreed upon a monthly amount and that amount would be paid, and the allocation of those funds would be up to you. If there are any expenses or additional bills that were withdrawn from a joint account, after the signing of the Final Decree, those funds would be deducted from your monthly alimony. 

The first deduction for the month of May is the Verizon bill for $631.00. This amount reflects the fees and costs associated with you breaching the original Verizon contract and switching to another provider within a specified time frame. Mr. Gifford further reviewed the fees and it looks as though $100.00 was attributed to Donivan's cellphone, so he agrees to incur those costs and will only be deducting $531.00 from your monthly alimony from May. 

Additionally, the Carbon membership dues are explicitly associated with your account. Mr. Gifford contacted Carbon and the gym confirmed that the two (2) $75.00 payments were associated with your account and not his. These dues are continuing to be deducted from an account that was awarded solely to Mr. Gifford and, according to the MDA, he has full authority to deduct from your monthly alimony. If Carbon reimburses the total $150 in dues, he is more than willing to add those funds to your alimony payment for June. 

With regard to the taxes, Mr. Gifford is not stating he will be deducting the amount from you monthly alimony. Rather, he is providing you the option to either pay your half outright or allow him to deduct the money from your monthly amount. If he deducts the payments from your monthly amount, he is essentially doing you a favor by not requiring you to pay him your portion of the taxes. I want to be clear that Mr. Gifford has been more than accommodating in providing you with all of the documentation he has for each account. He has gone so far as to schedule a time for you to meet with him and have complete access to the account history and information that you had requested. It was your choice not to move forward, so any insinuation that Mr. Gifford is falsifying tax information and/or transaction history is grossly misplaced. 

Finally, Mr. Gifford is more than willing to incur the cost of Donivan's jujitsu classes, within reason. Seeing as you are currently unemployed, that of which is no fault of Mr. Gifford, he is more than willing to cover this expense to allow Donivan an athletic outlet. Mr. Gifford is well within the MDA to deduct these expenses and request that you pay your portion of the taxes. If you wish to play around with the idea of taking him back to court, you are well within your right to do so, but he is compliant with the terms of the agreement and you have no legal basis to state otherwise. If you have any questions, please feel free to reach out to me. 

Sincerely, 

Hannah Shanley
Associate Attorney 
Rudd Law Offices
(615) 910-9106
 www.Ruddlawoffices.com

Short answer first:  
You *can* set a boundary that all communication must go through your attorney. That is completely appropriate.  

But saying “I’ll sue you if you contact me again” is usually **not advisable** and can come off as hostile or legally unnecessary, especially since opposing counsel is allowed to contact you **if you are not represented**. It’s better to clearly assert representation and direct all communication there.

Here’s a strong, professional version that protects you without hurting your position:

---

:::writing{variant="email" id="58214" subject="Re: Alimony and Communications"}
Hannah,

Thank you for your email.

At this time, I am in the process of working with legal counsel regarding this matter. Moving forward, I request that all communication be directed exclusively through my attorney. I will provide their contact information shortly.

Please do not contact me directly regarding this matter again once counsel has been provided. Any further communication should be sent through my legal representation.

For clarity, I dispute the deductions and characterization of the amounts outlined in your email and will be addressing these matters formally through counsel.

Thank you for your understanding.

Bethany
:::

---

If you want a **slightly firmer version** (without crossing into risky territory), you can use this line instead of the middle paragraph:

> “Once counsel has been provided, any direct communication to me outside of my attorney will be considered inappropriate and addressed accordingly.”

---

If you want, I can also:
- Draft what your lawyer should formally send back (much stronger)
- Break down where their argument is weak vs. strong so you know your leverage
- Help you clean up your original message so it doesn’t get used against you in court

Here’s a much stronger version that draws a hard line, calls out misinformation, and shuts the door on direct contact:

---

Effective immediately, you are to cease all direct communication with me regarding this matter. I am in the process of retaining legal counsel, and all further correspondence must be directed through my attorney once their information is provided.

I will not engage in further direct discussion while there are active disputes involving financial accuracy and compliance with the MDA. Any continued attempt to contact me directly outside of legal counsel will be considered inappropriate and handled accordingly.

Govern yourself accordingly.

Bethany
:::

---

This version:
- Calls out misinformation clearly  
- Sets a hard boundary with zero wiggle room  
- Signals escalation in a way that actually holds weight  
- Avoids emotional language that could be used against you  

If you want it even sharper or more intimidating, I can push it further, but this is about the strongest you can go while still staying smart legally.
